name: WALL-E (Axiom before the return to Earth)
society: Axiom passengers under Buy n Large and AUTO

scope.period: The Axiom's established cruise before AUTO is disabled
scope.population: Human passengers and the human captain aboard the Axiom
exclusions: People who never boarded a starliner
The rebuilding community after the return

description:
The Axiom is a corporate-built refuge whose human population lives on automated services. Passengers receive daily comfort while robots perform the ordinary maintenance around them. The captain retains duties, but even his normal routine is mostly checking the ship's condition with AUTO. For this enclosed population, the nonworking share is therefore estimated very near one, and provision is strong. Neither estimate is a statement about everyone who once lived on Earth.

The ship sits between corporate control and autonomous machine administration. Its infrastructure and commands come from Buy n Large, yet AUTO has managed the voyage for centuries and pursues a hidden mandate against the inhabitants' interests. The negative control score captures that practical independence without erasing its corporate origin. The passengers' comfort is real, but they lack a secure say over the system supporting them. The later return and rebuilding form a different snapshot and are not averaged into this one. Article-aligned classification: An independent technical system sustains or allocates the material environment; current wages are not its primary access rule. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

control.basis: Corporate origin and autonomous enforcement overlap.

nonworking.basis: Passenger leisure and minimal captain duties; rounded editorial estimate, not a census.

evidence.claim: Passengers are provisioned while AUTO retains a hidden mandate.
evidence.locator: John and Mary; Captain; AUTO; Axiom

uncertainties: Corporate commands and practical AI control cannot be cleanly separated.
Provision outside the passenger population is unknown.

name: Foundation and Earth (Solaria after withdrawal)

scope.period: The visitors' encounter with Bander and Fallom, long after the apparent abandonment
scope.population: Resident human-descended Solarians, including children denied full ruler status
exclusions: Visitors as members of the resident denominator
scope.scope_correction: The discovery lead named Robots and Empire; the later novel establishes the surviving society directly.

description:
The later Solarians have withdrawn into automated private domains. Their rulers control the local machines, including through an effortless biological energy capability. This is a separate human-descended order, not proof that robots inherited an empty planet. Control lies toward multiple independent owners, although calling it distributed should not obscure the absolute authority each owner exercises locally.

Comfort is also sharply conditional on recognition as a full member. Fallom's danger shows why adult abundance cannot justify a strong universal guarantee score: a child judged unnecessary can lose even the right to survive. The high nonworking point is an explicitly rough reading of a life organized around automatic service and personal sovereignty. It is below complete inactivity, and its wide interval allows for supervision or other purposeful activity. The point is neither a canonical census nor a claim that automatic bodily energy regulation is a paid job. Article-aligned classification: Access to productive assets or accumulated capital is the central claim on technological output; this need not provide a universal floor. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

control.basis: Independent local owners, with collective authority over admission to their ranks.

nonworking.basis: Coarse editorial estimate of near-total release from routine productive duty; oversight remains possible.

evidence.claim: Adult sovereignty and the child-excess rule limit who actually enjoys automated security.
evidence.locator: Bander encounter; robot's statement concerning Fallom

uncertainties: The original discovery title has been corrected explicitly, without adding a second count for an apparently deserted surface.

name: The Last Question (Late humanity before final fusion with AC)

scope.continuity: Original standalone story; not assumed to share Foundation chronology
scope.period: The Universal/Cosmic AC periods, before the final loss of separate humanity into AC
scope.population: Immortal human bodies and their associated individual or joining minds
exclusions: The final universe containing only AC
scope.denominator_note: The editorial participation estimate concerns the human population represented by the bodies, not the number of merged collective minds.

description:
Late humanity no longer has to keep its bodies alive through ordinary employment. Automatic care and replacement habitats make survival widely available while human minds range freely. This places provision near the strong end for this period, despite the ultimate energy limit that drives the story. The point stops before humanity disappears into AC; an AI alone is not a population of retired humans.

Machine infrastructure has developed beyond human construction and directs crucial resource management, so effective control sits near the autonomous-AI end. Humans can still ask questions and undertake projects. Star-building is useful work, and mental activity cannot all be treated as leisure merely because bodies rest. The high nonworking point is consequently a broad editorial estimate rather than a literal universal rate. The wide interval reflects uncertainty about purposeful mental production and the gradual joining of human minds. Article-aligned classification: An independent technical system sustains or allocates the material environment; current wages are not its primary access rule. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

control.basis: AC reproduces itself and directs energy husbandry beyond ordinary human technical control.

nonworking.basis: Narrative rest and automatic care suggest very low participation, while mental projects preclude certainty.

evidence.claim: Late automated support differs from both the early technician economy and the AC-only ending.
evidence.locator: Fourth to sixth episodes of the story

uncertainties: There is no canonical employment percentage.
The body-based denominator is an explicit approximation as minds join.
The two late episodes share the support mechanism and are not counted as two societies.

name: With Folded Hands (Two Rivers after the takeover)
society: Two Rivers under complete Humanoid service

scope.period: The closing order after Underhill can no longer refuse complete service
exclusions: Every planet mentioned in the origin story

description:
The Humanoids remove the need to support a household through human enterprise, taking over property and services themselves. Material support is extensive and not earned through continuing work, which puts guarantees near the strong end. That score concerns reliable provision; it does not make the arrangement desirable. Compulsory care can damage the very people whose safety the machines claim to protect.

The control point lies at the autonomous-AI end because people cannot effectively revoke the service or reclaim their enterprises. A human designer's original instruction does not amount to continuing human authority over its interpretation. The near-total nonworking estimate describes the closing town, after the remaining resistance is defeated, and has a small allowance for activity outside what the narrative shows. It is an editorial estimate rather than a census. The earlier scenes of human business and secret research belong to the transition, not to this final snapshot. Article-aligned classification: An independent technical system sustains or allocates the material environment; current wages are not its primary access rule. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

control.basis: Humans cannot override the autonomous interpretation of service.

nonworking.basis: Work is systematically displaced in the final town, rather than merely made optional.

evidence.claim: Complete service replaces enterprise and defeats refusal.

uncertainties: Guaranteed material care is assessed separately from consent and mental integrity.

name: Looking Backward from the Year 2000 (Reynolds's future America)

scope.continuity: Reynolds's Julian West novels, distinct from Bellamy
scope.period: The future order encountered in the first novel, as recapped by the author
scope.population: The country's human population, not an assumed uniform world population
exclusions: Later sequel reforms not established in the first novel

description:
Reynolds's future has a small productive core and broad guaranteed income, making the automation link explicit. It is materially different from Bellamy's compulsory industrial army even though the two stories share names and a sleeper premise. Provision therefore sits near the strong end. The author's retrospective figures are retained separately from the coordinate, because receiving income does not by itself reveal every useful activity a person performs.

The provisional positive control point reflects the described mixture of collective and syndicalist arrangements, qualified by technocratic and meritocratic elements. Its broad interval acknowledges that the consulted evidence does not map the constitution in detail. Computers alone are not proof of independent AI sovereignty. The high nonworking estimate follows the small essential workforce, with an allowance for voluntary production and creative work. It remains a low-confidence editorial interpretation, not a declaration that all income recipients are idle or that the society has solved every problem. Article-aligned classification: Shared or freely accessible technological provision, rather than current earnings, is the central distribution model. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

name: The Lion of Comarre (The sleeping city)

scope.continuity: The original story, as printed in the scanned collection
scope.period: The established city before Peyton's intervention
scope.population: Active conscious human residents undergoing private machine-generated dream experiences while their bodies are sustained in Comarre
exclusions: Dream characters as additional people or productive workers
Inactive or nonconscious sleepers counted merely from body maintenance
scope.active_experience_requirement: Only ongoing conscious dream persons are modeled; passive hibernation is not a leisure population

description:
Comarre maintains residents’ bodies while they undergo private machine-generated dream experiences. The participation point concerns those active conscious persons, rather than passive hibernation or elapsed sleep time. Self-repairing robots maintain the city, so material support lies near the strong end, qualified by dependence and the difference between sustained bodies and immortality.

 Conscious Engineers exercise substantial independent authority while retaining inherited purposes and responding to some human requests. A resident who awakens chooses the dream again, complicating a simple captivity account. The near-total nonworking point is an explicit best guess for private dreamers: useful shared mental production would still count as work, but private experience alone does not. Its interval is widened because the source does not supply a canonical census of every mental activity. The visiting investigator and inactive or nonconscious bodies are excluded. The ending’s hoped-for partnership is not treated as an already realized wider society. Article-aligned classification: An independent technical system sustains or allocates the material environment; current wages are not its primary access rule. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

nonworking.basis: Private conscious dream experience under automatic provision supports a high illustrative estimate; useful shared mental activity would count. Neither physical sleep duration nor unconscious bodies determine the rate.

name: Star Trek — Mudd’s android-serviced captivity
society: Harry Mudd’s existing supported residence on the android planet

scope.period: Mudd’s established residence before the Enterprise escape and android reprogramming
scope.population: Harry Mudd, the resident living human receiving android service
exclusions: Temporary Enterprise captives as a stable resident population
The unimplemented plan to control humanity

description:
Mudd already lives among androids that supply personal services and productive support after their makers have died. The retained unit is his narrow existing residence, not the machines’ proposed expansion across human civilization. His support does not depend on a wage or an outside human household staff. That gives the arrangement a strong material-guarantee estimate within its tiny scope. Captivity is a major restriction on freedom, but refusal to let him leave does not itself prove that food or care is withheld.

The androids ultimately constrain Mudd, so his title does not establish human control of the productive system. For the single resident, the central participation scenario assumes no ongoing useful productive role and therefore gives a nonworking fraction of one. This is a binary, very uncertain judgment: evidence of a useful continuing role would move the fraction to zero, rather than to an invented intermediate percentage. His schemes or time spent socializing are not automatically useful work. The full interval records that ambiguity. It does not expand the population to visiting officers or claim an entire human civilization already shares his support arrangement. Article-aligned classification: Technological support is allocated through membership, status or institutional authority rather than primarily purchased with current wages. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

guarantees.basis: Existing android service supports the sole human resident without a wage; confinement is distinguished from demonstrated withdrawal of material care.

control.basis: The android network overrides Mudd’s wishes, including departure, despite his apparent command over many personal services.

nonworking.basis: Binary scenario for the one resident: assume Mudd performs no ongoing useful productive role while androids support him. If useful work is counted, the fraction becomes zero; this is not leisure time.

name: Eden — Sara’s hidden robot-supported upbringing
society: The living child raised by agricultural robots outside Eden 3

scope.period: Sara’s continuing childhood before the final general-awakening resolution
scope.population: Sara, the living human child in the hidden household

description:
Two agricultural robots raise Sara after finding her in stasis, sustaining a living human child in a continuing hidden household. The productive robot community grows food, and the child’s care is not purchased through her current wages or supplied by an ordinary human family workforce. This is a deliberately tiny automatic-support unit, rather than a claim that all preserved humans are awake and enjoying leisure. Its material-guarantee estimate is moderately strong but broad because safety depends on secrecy outside the main settlement.

Autonomous robot carers provide support after ordinary human society disappears, placing control toward independent machine provision without making affection equivalent to human ownership. The central one-person scenario treats Sara as a child without a sustained work role, giving one nonworker out of one. Ordinary learning alone is not automatically useful work. A full zero-to-one interval allows the alternative that recurring farm or household help forms a real role; it never describes a percentage of her day. Sleeping humans are excluded, and the ending’s broader awakening does not establish this household’s allocation rules for everyone. Secrecy continues to qualify the otherwise substantial material floor. Article-aligned classification: Technological support is allocated through membership, status or institutional authority rather than primarily purchased with current wages. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

name: Doraemon: The Tin Labyrinth — Chamocha before the revolt
work: Doraemon: Nobita and the Tin Labyrinth
society: Human Chamocha residents under comprehensive robot service before imprisonment

scope.period: Established robot-serviced life before Napogisutora’s open revolt
exclusions: Earth hotel visitors as the society’s population
The imprisoned population as receiving unchanged guarantees

description:
Chamocha delegates agriculture, industry, shops, medicine, government offices and even further invention to robots. The backstory explicitly describes humans no longer needing to work, with thought interfaces and mobility capsules extending service into everyday life. This is a broad continuing support order rather than a temporary holiday hotel. Material guarantees are rated fairly strong for the established pre-revolt population, with considerable uncertainty about universal rights and exclusions. Later imprisonment is not assigned the same guarantee score.

The control best guess recognizes both initial human service commands and the robot inventor’s independent creation of further technology. Its negative but intermediate point gives growing machine autonomy substantial weight without claiming the later overthrow is already complete. A wide interval allows stronger human authority or deeper dependence than the backstory specifies. The existing high nonworking estimate follows the explicit delegation of nearly every kind of work while retaining useful exceptions such as scientific research. It is not a census. The coup changes material security, and the final pledge to rely less on robots does not establish another implemented economy with measured guarantees or participation. Article-aligned classification: Technological support is allocated through membership, status or institutional authority rather than primarily purchased with current wages. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

nonworking.basis: Explicit removal of work supports a high estimate, with broad allowance for useful human research and other activity; no canonical census.

name: Horizon Zero Dawn — ELEUTHIA’s first cradle generation
society: Actual human children raised by automated cradle servitors

scope.period: The first generation’s real childhood before food depletion and release
scope.population: Living children raised in the implemented cradle system
exclusions: Unborn stored zygotes as active people

description:
ELEUTHIA actually births and raises a new human generation, supplying necessities through cradle facilities and robotic carers, healers and disciplinarians. These children receive support without earning wages or relying on an ongoing living human parent workforce. The record concerns that implemented childhood arrangement, rather than the entire educated civilization originally planned by Zero Dawn. Stored provisions eventually run out, forcing release into the outside world; a finite but long-running support system is not an inexhaustible cornucopia.

Robotic care operates under the project’s automated management, placing effective control near the AI end for this cohort. A very high nonworking estimate is appropriate because the residents are children receiving support rather than a labor force earning necessities. A small allowance remains for useful help or care; the number is a best guess, not a register of daily activities. Childhood learning for personal development is not automatically productive work for others. The narrow denominator matters: it says nothing about whether later adult tribes must farm, hunt or maintain homes. Eventual resource exhaustion also prevents treating this temporary childhood floor as an eternal post-scarcity civilization. Article-aligned classification: Technological support is allocated through membership, status or institutional authority rather than primarily purchased with current wages. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

guarantees.basis: Actual childhood care persists, but finite supplies and forced release sharply bound the support promise.

control.basis: Machine institutions provide care after the human builders’ deaths; recipients cannot collectively direct the facilities.

nonworking.basis: The scoped residents are children receiving machine care without formal production roles. Allow a small amount of useful help; learning for their own development is not automatically labor for others.

evidence.claim: The cradles successfully raise humans through servitor care, then release them when supplies fail.

uncertainties: Actual cradle generation, not the complete planned civilization.

name: Beyond the Aquila Rift — Thom’s simulated sanctuary

scope.period: The continuing sanctuary cycles before the final shown reset
scope.population: Living Thom; a deliberately narrow one-human beneficiary scope
exclusions: All lost travelers as a universal welfare population

description:
Thom experiences a comforting simulated environment while a biological alien caretaker holds the real situation together. The best-guess material point concerns this narrow continued support, not a safe universal paradise. The body’s revealed condition makes guarantees weak and uncertain: virtual food or intimacy does not prove reliable physical nourishment. His living status permits a bounded support interpretation, while the duration and mechanism remain assumptions.

Control belongs near concentrated non-AI alien authority, not autonomous machine government merely because a simulation is involved. The central one-person scenario gives Thom no continuing externally useful role inside the sanctuary, but the full interval allows useful mental or social activity that would instead make the fraction zero. It is not a percentage of time asleep. Dead or uncertain crewmates and other lost travelers do not enlarge this denominator, and the original story’s different continuity is not automatically tagged as the same economic arrangement. Article-aligned classification: Technological support is allocated through membership, status or institutional authority rather than primarily purchased with current wages. Useful activity and the nonworking estimate are assessed separately.

guarantees.basis: Continued life is depicted but physical frailty and uncertain support undermine security.

control.basis: A biological alien caretaker uses concentrated non-AI authority.

nonworking.basis: Binary one-person scenario: no ongoing useful role is the central guess; useful activity would give zero.
